'''''Lepidium latifolium''''', known by several common names including '''perennial pepperweed''',<ref name=colorado>{{Cite web|url=https://www.colorado.gov/pacific/agconservation/perennial-pepperweed|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301134850/https://www.colorado.gov/pacific/agconservation/perennial-pepperweed|archive-date=March 1, 2017|title=Perennial pepperweed|date=September 17, 2014|website=Department of Agriculture – Conservation Services}}</ref> '''broadleaved pepperweed''', '''pepperwort''', '''peppergrass''',<ref name=usda>{{Cite web|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=LELA2|title=Plants Profile for Lepidium latifolium (broadleaved pepperweed)|website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> '''dittander''', '''dittany''', and '''tall whitetop''',<ref name=usda/> is a [[perennial]] plant that is a member of the [[Brassicaceae|mustard and cabbage family]].

==Description==
''Lepidium latifolium'' normally grows to {{convert|30-100|cm|in|abbr=on}}, but may grow as tall as {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}}. It has numerous woody stems, alternating waxy leaves and clusters of small white flowers. It produces small (1.6 mm) fruits which each contain two reddish seeds. It has an extensive root network, known to reach {{convert|9|ft|m|abbr=on}} in depth, and constituting 40% of the total [[Biomass (ecology)|biomass]] of the plant.<ref name=fs/>

==Distribution==
This plant is native to southern Europe, [[Mediterranean]] countries and Asia as far east as the [[Himalayas]]. It is an [[introduced species]] in Australia and North America, growing throughout the United States and Mexico. It may have been introduced to the U.S. when its seed got into a shipment of [[sugar beet]] seeds.<ref name=fs>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/forb/leplat/all.html|title=Lepidium latifolium|website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref>

==Invasive plant==
The plant is most [[invasive species|invasive]] in [[wetland]] habitats, including [[riparian zone]]s; from there it easily spreads to other ecosystems, such as [[sagebrush]].<ref name=fs/> It is perceived as a threat to [[salt marsh]]es in southern [[New Hampshire]], prompting the [[New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services|Department of Environmental Services]] and the [[U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service]] to look for it in the [[Hampton, New Hampshire|Hampton]]–[[Seabrook, New Hampshire|Seabrook]] Estuary in 2008, where it is thought to have spread. The agencies were recruiting volunteers to help look for and properly remove it from this area.<ref>{{cite news | title=NH looking for volunteers to stop invasive plant | publisher=[[Associated Press]] | date=2008-06-16 | url=http://www.seacoastonline.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20080616/NEWS/80616016/-1/NEWS19&sfad=1 | access-date=2008-06-17 | archive-date=2011-06-06 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606141447/http://www.seacoastonline.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20080616/NEWS/80616016/-1/NEWS19&sfad=1 }}</ref> It is also a pest in the [[Monte Vista National Wildlife Refuge|Monte Vista]] and [[Alamosa National Wildlife Refuge]]s in [[Colorado]] and [[Malheur National Wildlife Refuge]] in [[Oregon]], and many other sites.<ref name=fs/>

==Uses==
The leaves, shoots, and fruits of this plant are all edible. In Ladakh in the Himalayas, the spring leaves are prized as a vegetable. The peppery edge or bitterness is removed by first boiling the young shoots and leaves, and then soaking in water for two days. Cooked like spinach, it makes a nutritious vegetable.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kaur |first1=T |last2=Hussain |first2=K |last3=Koul |first3=S |last4=Vishwakarma |first4=R |last5=Vyas |first5=D |title=Evaluation of nutritional and antioxidant status of Lepidium latifolium Linn.: a novel phytofood from Ladakh. |journal=PLOS ONE |date=2013 |volume=8 |issue=8 |article-number=e69112 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0069112 |pmid=23936316|pmc=3732271 |bibcode=2013PLoSO...869112K |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The dried stems are sometimes used in flower arrangements.
